title: Sharing, federation and interoperability
summary: Compare copy, governed share, federation and clean room on six questions, trace an OpenSharing read from credential to file download, and place ingestion, UniForm, Iceberg catalogs and clean rooms at their boundaries.
objectives: Compare copy, governed share, federation and clean room on movement, enforcement, cost in kind, revocation, freshness and failure.
Trace an OpenSharing read from recipient credential to direct file download, and plan credentials and a revocation rehearsal.
Choose ingestion or access-in-place and explain UniForm, Iceberg catalogs and clean rooms as interoperability boundaries.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
Three patterns, one set of questions
OpenSharing: names, objects and the read path
Worked example: Cinderline to Halvern Coatings

questions.prompt: Last Monday Halvern saved a read of the shared view to a CSV on an engineer's laptop. Today Cinderline removes Halvern's grant and rotates its token with zero seconds. What happens to the CSV?

options.text: Nothing: revocation stops future requests and cannot reach bytes already saved.
options.rationale: The CSV is a copy in Halvern's systems; only the agreement's retention terms govern it.

options.text: It becomes unreadable because the token it came from has expired.
options.rationale: A saved file is not encrypted with the token; the token only authorized the original request.

options.text: It is deleted at the next file-URL expiry.
options.rationale: URL expiry ends the link to Cinderline's storage, not files already downloaded.

options.text: It refreshes to an empty file on next open.
options.rationale: A local CSV never contacts the sharing server, so nothing can change it.

questions.prompt: A federated query's EXPLAIN FORMATTED shows that the remote query sent to the MES database has no WHERE clause, although your SQL filters on a Databricks function of order_code. What does that mean for the run?

options.text: The source returns every row for the selected columns and Databricks applies the filter after transfer.
options.rationale: Only predicates present in the remote query run at the source; the rest run locally.

options.text: The source will apply the filter from its own statistics.
options.rationale: The source executes only the query text it receives; it has no copy of your predicate.

options.text: The query is rejected because the predicate cannot be pushed.
options.rationale: Non-pushable predicates are evaluated in Databricks; the query still runs.

options.text: Raising fetchSize will make the source filter.
options.rationale: fetchSize changes rows per batch, not which predicates the source evaluates.

questions.prompt: A supplier has a Unity Catalog-enabled workspace. What does it give Cinderline so that Cinderline can create a recipient that needs no token?

options.text: Its sharing identifier, in the form cloud:region:metastore-uuid.
options.rationale: Databricks-to-Databricks recipients are created from the recipient metastore's identifier, with no credential file.

options.text: An activation link to download its credential file.
options.rationale: Activation links are what a provider sends to open-sharing recipients, not what a recipient sends.

options.text: A bearer token for Cinderline's sharing server.
options.rationale: Bearer tokens belong to open sharing; this mode exchanges none.

options.text: The URL of its SQL warehouse.
options.rationale: A warehouse address is not a sharing identity; the metastore identifier is.

cards.prompt: After a CSV export reaches a supplier, which controls does Cinderline still have over it?
cards.answer: None technical: the copy is enforced only by the holder's own controls and by the agreement.
cards.explanation: A copy carries no link back to Cinderline's catalog or sharing server, so it cannot be revoked and no read of it is recorded on Cinderline's side. That is why a copy needs written retention and deletion terms, and why a governed share is preferred when access must be withdrawable.

cards.prompt: Documentation now says OpenSharing. Which strings in a recipient's code must stay exactly as they are?
cards.answer: The Spark format deltaSharing, the delta_sharing package, the profile's field names and the API resources shares, recipients and providers.
cards.explanation: A product name in documentation is prose; identifiers are registered names that code resolves at run time. The open protocol specification is still titled Delta Sharing Protocol, so a mechanical rename breaks connectors without changing any behaviour. Use OpenSharing in explanations and keep every identifier verbatim.

cards.prompt: Why should a group rather than a single person own a share?
cards.answer: Because recipients can read a shared table only while the share owner keeps SELECT on it.
cards.explanation: The Databricks API reference says the owner's SELECT on each shared table must be maintained indefinitely. If an individual owner leaves and loses access, the shared object reports permission denied and every recipient's reads fail, although the grant and recipient are unchanged. A group owner survives staff changes.

cards.prompt: What does a supplier with a Unity Catalog workspace give Cinderline, and what replaces the token?
cards.answer: Its sharing identifier, cloud:region:metastore-uuid; its own metastore authenticates, so no token is exchanged.
cards.explanation: In Databricks-to-Databricks sharing the recipient object is created with the recipient's global metastore identifier. The supplier's admin then creates a catalog from the share and grants it to its own users like any catalog. No credential file exists to leak or rotate, which is the main operational difference from open sharing.

cards.prompt: A recipient's credential profile has no expirationTime field. What does that mean for Cinderline's risk?
cards.answer: The protocol treats the bearer token as never expiring, so whoever holds the file can read until Cinderline acts.
cards.explanation: The profile carries the endpoint and bearer token, and expirationTime is optional. Without an expiry, a forwarded or leaked file stays valid indefinitely. Set an expiry on the recipient's token, restrict source addresses with its IP access list, rotate before expiry, and rotate with zero seconds if the file is ever mis-sent.

cards.prompt: When a supplier reads a shared table, where do the Parquet bytes come from?
cards.answer: Directly from Cinderline's cloud storage, through short-lived file URLs or temporary credentials the sharing server issued.
cards.explanation: The sharing server authorizes the request and returns file locations, not data; the client then downloads from the provider's storage. So transfer out of Cinderline's storage region lands on the storage owner's cloud bill, and a download does not re-check the grant: the URL's own expiry is the limit.

cards.prompt: When does a supplier's view of a shared table become stale?
cards.answer: As soon as it works from anything it saved while Cinderline has committed a newer version.
cards.explanation: Each protocol read returns the latest version, so a query is fresh when it runs. A DataFrame, extract or dashboard cache made from that read is a copy and ages from the moment it is written. The protocol's table-version call is the cheap way for a client to detect that its cache is behind.

cards.prompt: List what revoking a recipient stops immediately and what it cannot reach.
cards.answer: It stops the next request; it cannot recall already-issued file URLs before they expire, or anything the recipient saved.
cards.explanation: Removing the grant, deleting the recipient or rotating with zero seconds makes the next REST call fail. File URLs issued earlier carry their own expiration timestamps, and copies live in the recipient's systems. Revocation therefore needs a rehearsal that measures the tail, and an agreement that covers retention.

cards.prompt: A Cinderline analyst queries a foreign table. Which two authorizations does the query pass?
cards.answer: Unity Catalog checks the analyst's grants on the foreign catalog; the source checks the connection's credential.
cards.explanation: The connection stores the source's host and credential options once. Unity Catalog decides which people may use the foreign catalog, and the source database decides what the connection's database user may read. The source's log therefore shows the connection's user, not the analyst; per-person evidence lives on the Databricks side.

cards.prompt: How do you show that a filter in a federated query ran in the source database?
cards.answer: Read the remote query in EXPLAIN FORMATTED; if the predicate is absent, Databricks filters after fetching the rows.
cards.explanation: Connectors translate some predicates, projections and limits into the SQL they send and keep others local. The remote query text is the evidence of what the source ran; a missing predicate means every row of the unfiltered query crossed the network. JDBC fetchSize only changes batch size, not parallelism.

cards.prompt: When is ingesting a copy better than access-in-place for a partner's data?
cards.answer: When the data is queried often, needs history the source will not keep, or the source must not carry query load.
cards.explanation: An ingested Delta table answers repeated queries quickly, keeps versions, and loads the source once per run; a source outage delays one load instead of breaking every query. Access-in-place wins for occasional questions that need the source's current state. The copy must then be owned, retained and deleted deliberately.

cards.prompt: Why can an Iceberg engine reading a UniForm table see older rows than a Delta reader?
cards.answer: Iceberg metadata is generated asynchronously after each Delta commit, so it can trail by one or more versions.
cards.explanation: UniForm writes Iceberg metadata for the same Parquet files after the Delta transaction completes and may bundle frequent commits. The converted_delta_version property records the last Delta version the Iceberg metadata reflects, so comparing it with the Delta version is the first check before suspecting lost data.

cards.prompt: A service principal owns a schema and holds ALL PRIVILEGES, yet an external engine gets no vended credentials. Why?
cards.answer: Vending needs EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA granted explicitly by the catalog owner, plus external access enabled on the metastore.
cards.explanation: The Databricks API reference states that EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA is not included in schema ownership or ALL PRIVILEGES, for security reasons, and that the metastore's external access flag is off by default. Both keep engines outside Databricks from receiving storage credentials unless someone deliberately decided they should.

cards.prompt: In a clean room, what actually leaves for each collaborator?
cards.answer: Only what the approved notebook writes to the output catalog; the row-level assets stay inside.
cards.explanation: Collaborators add tables and code but cannot open each other's data directly. A notebook is reviewed and run by named collaborators, and its outputs are the exit. A notebook that writes joined raw rows would leak them, so reviewers check output columns and aggregation, not only the room's configuration.

cards.prompt: Why decide the sharing pattern separately for each direction of a partnership?
cards.answer: Because each direction has its own owner, tooling, load tolerance and revocation need, so the best pattern often differs.
cards.explanation: In the worked example Cinderline shares a view to Halvern because Halvern may see the rows and Cinderline must be able to cut access, while Halvern's batch parameters come back as a weekly extract because its DBA refuses query load. One pattern for both directions would break one side's constraint.
